Issues.Title: BertTokenizer and tokenizer.json normalizers throw ArgumentException on noncharacters
Issues.Body:
**System Information (please complete the following information):**
 - OS & Version: Windows 11, with ICU and NLS
 - ML.NET Version: Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers 3.0.0, and main at 218d0b8, which includes #7954
 - .NET Version: .NET 10.0 and .NET Framework 4.8

**Describe the bug**
The tokenizers call `string.Normalize` on the text, and it throws `ArgumentException` ("String contains invalid Unicode code points") on noncharacters:
- With NLS, on noncharacters like U+FFFF, U+FDD0 and U+1FFFE. .NET Framework always uses NLS, and .NET uses it with `DOTNET_SYSTEM_GLOBALIZATION_USENLS`. `BertTokenizer` throws with or without `RemoveNonSpacingMarks`, and so do the `StripAccents` and Unicode normalization steps of `SentencePieceTokenizer.CreateFromTokenizerJson`.
- With ICU, on U+FFFE. #7954 fixed this for `BertTokenizer`, but the tokenizer.json steps still throw.

**To Reproduce**
```csharp
using System.Text;
using Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers;

File.WriteAllLines("vocab.txt", new[] { "[PAD]", "[UNK]", "[CLS]", "[SEP]", "[MASK]", "one", "line", "##line" });
BertTokenizer.Create("vocab.txt").EncodeToIds("one\uFFFFline"); // ArgumentException with NLS

string json = """
    {
      "normalizer": { "type": "NFKC" },
      "pre_tokenizer": { "type": "Metaspace", "replacement": "\u2581", "add_prefix_space": true },
      "model": { "type": "Unigram", "unk_id": 0, "vocab": [["<unk>", 0.0], ["\u2581one", -1.0], ["line", -1.0]] }
    }
    """;
var tokenizer = SentencePieceTokenizer.CreateFromTokenizerJson(new MemoryStream(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(json)));
tokenizer.EncodeToIds("one\uFFFFline"); // ArgumentException with NLS
tokenizer.EncodeToIds("one\uFFFEline"); // ArgumentException, also with ICU
```

For NLS, run it with `DOTNET_SYSTEM_GLOBALIZATION_USENLS=1`, or on .NET Framework, where the message is "Invalid Unicode code point found at index 3".

**Expected behavior**
No exception. Noncharacters should work the way U+FFFF does with ICU: on main, `BertTokenizer` gives `[UNK]`, and the tokenizer.json steps keep it unchanged.

**Screenshots, Code, Sample Projects**
Both normalizers already handle lone surrogates, and `BertNormalizer` also handles U+FFFE, but not the other noncharacters:

https://github.com/dotnet/machinelearning/blob/218d0b825ff02e800b8944e17f5b80da11950960/src/Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers/Normalizer/BertNormalizer.cs#L139

https://github.com/dotnet/machinelearning/blob/218d0b825ff02e800b8944e17f5b80da11950960/src/Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers/Normalizer/SentencePieceNormalizationStep.cs#L314

Noncharacters don't change under normalization and don't combine with the characters around them, so one option is to normalize the text between them and keep them as they are.

**Additional context**
- I found this while fixing #7950 in #7954, which only handles what ICU rejects: U+FFFE and lone surrogates.
- With `RemoveNonSpacingMarks`, `BertNormalizer` also calls `string.Normalize` at the start ([L39](https://github.com/dotnet/machinelearning/blob/218d0b825ff02e800b8944e17f5b80da11950960/src/Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers/Normalizer/BertNormalizer.cs#L39)). So removing the final NFC, as #7957 proposes, would fix `BertTokenizer` with the default options, but not with `RemoveNonSpacingMarks`.

Issues.Title: SentencePieceTokenizer: Unigram ties in multi-word text differ from Hugging Face
Issues.Body:
`SentencePieceTokenizer.CreateFromTokenizerJson` (Unigram) can still pick a different split than Hugging Face `tokenizers` when several splits have the same total score and the text has more than one word. #7956 fixes the single-word case from #7909 by scoring in double precision like Hugging Face, but not this one.

Hugging Face scores each pre-tokenized word on its own, starting from zero. `SentencePieceUnigramModel` scores the whole normalized string in one pass, so the running total from earlier words changes how ties in later words round.

Repro with the `Paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2` `tokenizer.json` from the test data, with #7956 applied:

```csharp
using var stream = File.OpenRead("tokenizer.json");
var tokenizer = SentencePieceTokenizer.CreateFromTokenizerJson(stream, addBeginningOfSentence: false, addEndOfSentence: false);
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(", ", tokenizer.EncodeToIds("a test9999999")));
```

| Input | ML.NET | Hugging Face `tokenizers` 0.23.3 |
|---|---|---|
| `a test9999999` | `[10, 3034, 5046, 5046, 65040]` (`▁a`, `▁test`, `99`, `99`, `999`) | `[10, 3034, 5046, 65040, 5046]` (`▁a`, `▁test`, `99`, `999`, `99`) |

`test9999999` on its own already gives the Hugging Face result.

Scoring each pre-tokenized word separately, like Hugging Face, matched it on every input I checked. `Create` with a `.model` stream should keep scoring the whole string, since that's what SentencePiece does.

Issues.Title: Throw when a tokenizer needs Unicode normalization in invariant mode
Issues.Body:
In globalization-invariant mode, `string.Normalize` returns its input unchanged, so `BertOptions.RemoveNonSpacingMarks` and the `StripAccents`, `NFC`, `NFD`, `NFKC` and `NFKD` normalizer steps loaded by `SentencePieceTokenizer.CreateFromTokenizerJson` silently skipped the Unicode normalization they rely on. For example, accents on precomposed characters were kept, so with uncased BERT vocabularies, words like "café" could become `[UNK]`. Creating such a tokenizer now throws `PlatformNotSupportedException`, pointing to https://aka.ms/GlobalizationInvariantMode.

There's no public API to detect invariant mode yet (dotnet/runtime#81429), so the check is whether `string.Normalize` decomposes "é".

In invariant mode, apps that use the option or these steps now fail when creating the tokenizer, instead of silently getting different tokens than with ICU. #7938 tried carrying our own Unicode data so that accent stripping works in invariant mode, and was closed in favor of failing loudly.

The NFC at the end of `BertNormalizer` doesn't throw, since it runs for every `BertTokenizer` with the default normalizer and only matters for text that isn't already NFC. #7957 proposes removing it.

Fixes #7728

Issues.Title: BertTokenizer throws ArgumentException on lone surrogates and U+FFFE
Issues.Body:
**System Information (please complete the following information):**
 - OS & Version: Windows, with both ICU and NLS. Nothing throws in globalization-invariant mode.
 - ML.NET Version: Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers from main at 755131b, which includes #7820. It also throws before #7820.
 - .NET Version: .NET 8.0 and .NET 10.0

**Describe the bug**
`BertTokenizer` throws `ArgumentException` ("String contains invalid Unicode code points") when the text contains:
- a lone surrogate and `RemoveNonSpacingMarks` is on
- U+FFFE, with any options

A lone surrogate is easy to hit, for example when a text is cut into chunks in the middle of an emoji.

Both come from `string.Normalize` in `BertNormalizer`: the NFD at the start (only with `RemoveNonSpacingMarks`) and the NFC at the end reject these characters. #7820 drops lone surrogates in the normalizer loop, but with `RemoveNonSpacingMarks` the NFD runs before that loop. In globalization-invariant mode `string.Normalize` returns its input unchanged, so nothing throws there.

**To Reproduce**
```csharp
using Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers;

var tokenizer = BertTokenizer.Create("vocab.txt", new BertOptions { RemoveNonSpacingMarks = true });
tokenizer.EncodeToIds("one\uD83Dline"); // ArgumentException

BertTokenizer.Create("vocab.txt").EncodeToIds("one\uFFFEline"); // ArgumentException
```

**Expected behavior**
No exception. Both characters should be dropped, the same way `BertNormalizer` already drops U+FFFD. Hugging Face gives `[UNK]` for U+FFFE, but it's a noncharacter, so dropping it is fine.

**Screenshots, Code, Sample Projects**
A fix on top of #7938, which changes the same line:

```csharp
// string.Normalize throws on lone surrogates and U+FFFE. The loop below removes U+FFFD.
original = _isNormalizationSupported
    ? SentencePieceNormalizationStep.ReplaceLoneSurrogates(original).Replace('\uFFFE', '\uFFFD').Normalize(NormalizationForm.FormD)
    : NonSpacingMarkRemover.Remove(original);
```

`SentencePieceNormalizationStep.ReplaceLoneSurrogates` also needs to become `internal`, and the check at the top of the loop that skips U+0000 and U+FFFD needs `|| c == '\uFFFE'`.

A regression test for `BertTokenizerTests`, using `AssertTokens` and the vocabulary from #7820. With #7938 applied, it fails without the fix and passes with it, with ICU and in invariant mode.

<details>
<summary>Test</summary>

```csharp
// string.Normalize throws on a lone surrogate, as in a text cut in the middle of an emoji, and on U+FFFE, as in UTF-16 read
// with the wrong byte order.
[Theory]
[InlineData(0xD83D, false)]
[InlineData(0xD83D, true)]
[InlineData(0xDC4D, true)]
[InlineData(0xFFFE, false)]
[InlineData(0xFFFE, true)]
public void TestLoneSurrogatesAndUFFFEAreRemoved(int c, bool removeNonSpacingMarks)
{
    AssertTokens($"one{(char)c}line", "[CLS] one ##line [SEP]", new BertOptions { RemoveNonSpacingMarks = removeNonSpacingMarks });
    AssertTokens($"great product {(char)c}", "[CLS] great product [SEP]", new BertOptions { RemoveNonSpacingMarks = removeNonSpacingMarks });
}
```

</details>

**Additional context**
I found this while reviewing #7820 and kept it out of that PR, because the fix overlaps with my PR #7938. I'll fix it once #7938 is merged.

Issues.Title: BertTokenizer recomposes Korean after stripping accents, so it gives `[UNK]` with uncased multilingual BERT
Issues.Body:
**System Information (please complete the following information):**
 - OS & Version: Windows 11, with both ICU and NLS
 - ML.NET Version: Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers 3.0.0, and main has the same code
 - .NET Version: .NET 10.0

**Describe the bug**
With `RemoveNonSpacingMarks = true`, `BertNormalizer` decomposes the text (NFD) and drops the non-spacing marks. NFD splits each Hangul syllable into jamo, which aren't marks, so they stay. But `Normalize` ends with an NFC, which puts the jamo back together into syllables.

Hugging Face doesn't recompose, so its uncased vocabularies have Korean as jamo. The `vocab.txt` of [bert-base-multilingual-uncased](https://huggingface.co/google-bert/bert-base-multilingual-uncased) has 1,459 tokens with jamo and none with Hangul syllables, so every Korean word becomes `[UNK]`.

**To Reproduce**
1. Create a console app:
   ```
   dotnet new console
   dotnet add package Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers --version 3.0.0
   ```
2. Download [`vocab.txt`](https://huggingface.co/google-bert/bert-base-multilingual-uncased/resolve/main/vocab.txt) of bert-base-multilingual-uncased into the project folder. Its tokenizer lowercases and strips accents, which in ML.NET is `RemoveNonSpacingMarks = true` (lowercasing is on by default).
3. Replace `Program.cs` with:
   ```csharp
   using Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers;

   var vocab = File.ReadAllLines("vocab.txt");
   var tokenizer = BertTokenizer.Create("vocab.txt", new BertOptions { RemoveNonSpacingMarks = true });

   var ids = tokenizer.EncodeToIds("서울은 한국의 수도입니다.");
   Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", ids.Select(id => vocab[id])));
   Console.WriteLine(string.Join(" ", ids));
   ```
4. `dotnet run` prints:
   ```
   [CLS] [UNK] [UNK] [UNK] . [SEP]
   101 100 100 100 119 102
   ```

**Expected behavior**
The same tokens as Hugging Face. With its `tokenizers` package (`pip install tokenizers`):
```python
from tokenizers import Tokenizer

tokenizer = Tokenizer.from_pretrained("google-bert/bert-base-multilingual-uncased")
encoding = tokenizer.encode("서울은 한국의 수도입니다.")
print(" ".join(encoding.tokens))
print(" ".join(map(str, encoding.ids)))
```
```
[CLS] 서울 ##은 한국 ##의 수도 ##입 ##니다 . [SEP]
101 47403 11375 47529 10576 66548 62776 82566 119 102
```
The Korean tokens look like syllables, but they're jamo: `서울` is U+1109 U+1165 U+110B U+116E U+11AF.

**Screenshots, Code, Sample Projects**
The NFC is at the end of `BertNormalizer.Normalize`:

https://github.com/dotnet/machinelearning/blob/ef195ab05cf522aacb894e2f78df914ea567a321/src/Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers/Normalizer/BertNormalizer.cs#L138

Hugging Face's `BertNormalizer` decomposes and strips the marks, but doesn't recompose: [bert.rs](https://github.com/huggingface/tokenizers/blob/b2b0d6067c8c1f6061cb4ae2dee04857921cb373/tokenizers/tk-encode/src/normalizers/bert.rs#L159-L169).

If I skip that NFC, with a custom `Normalizer` that otherwise does the same for this text, I get exactly Hugging Face's IDs, so removing it should fix this.

**Additional context**
- It's not only Korean. With `RemoveNonSpacingMarks = true`, 28 other characters are recomposed the same way, for example the Bengali vowel sign U+09CB. With cased models, the NFC changes 1,118 characters that Hugging Face leaves as they are, mostly CJK compatibility ideographs (U+F900 becomes U+8C48), and it also composes decomposed accents. Removing the NFC makes those match Hugging Face too.
- Without that NFC, the default `BertTokenizer` wouldn't call `string.Normalize` at all, so it would behave the same in globalization-invariant mode (#7728). It's also the NFC that throws on U+FFFE when `RemoveNonSpacingMarks` is false (#7950).

Issues.Title: Use double precision for Unigram scores loaded from tokenizer.json
Issues.Body:
`CreateFromTokenizerJson` can split text into the same Unigram pieces as Hugging Face `tokenizers` but in a different order, for example `aaaaaaaaaaaa` becomes `▁a aaaaa aaaaa a` instead of `▁a a aaaaa aaaaa`. This happens when several splits have the same total score: the scores are read and added up as `float`, like SentencePiece does, while Hugging Face [keeps them as `f64`](https://github.com/huggingface/tokenizers/blob/301277072263fb3830eb66eec7e47adadf76f1dc/tokenizers/src/models/unigram/model.rs#L255-L313), so rounding breaks the tie differently. Scores from `tokenizer.json` are now read and added up as `double`.

Reading the scores as `float` and only adding them up as `double` isn't enough, since many `tokenizer.json` scores aren't exact `float` values. `Create` with a `.model` stream or a `float` vocabulary still scores like SentencePiece and gives the same output as before, so on such ties it can now differ from `CreateFromTokenizerJson` for the same model.

Fixes #7909

Issues.Title: Add Hugging Face section to the tokenizers migration guide
Issues.Body:
Contributes to #7384

The tokenizers migration guide only covered moving from Microsoft.DeepDev.TokenizerLib to Tiktoken. This adds a section for people coming from the Hugging Face `transformers` and `tokenizers` Python packages: which `Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers` type to use for a model, which of its files you need, and how to get the same token IDs as in Python.

## Changes

- A table that maps each Hugging Face tokenizer to the `Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers` type that replaces it, with the model files it needs. It covers BERT, GPT-2, RoBERTa, CodeGen and Phi-2, Llama 2, T5 and XLM-RoBERTa.
- An example for each type that gives the same IDs as Python, with notes on where the results differ. When an issue tracks a difference, the note links to it.
- How to load a model that only has `tokenizer.json`. `SentencePieceTokenizer.CreateFromTokenizerJson` reads Unigram models. There's no loader for WordPiece and BPE models, so the guide shows how to read their settings from `tokenizer.json`.
- A table of common operations, like `add_special_tokens=False`, `decode` and truncation, and what to use instead.
- A link to #7735, which tracks a factory like `AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained`.
- The intro no longer says the guide is only for Tiktoken.

## Tests

This only changes docs. To check the examples:

- I ran every code block in the new section, taken from the markdown file, against the Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers 3.0.0 package and against a build of main at 696d6015d. I compared the IDs with `transformers` 5.24.0 and `tokenizers` 0.23.3 for 10 models: bert-base-uncased, bert-base-cased, all-MiniLM-L6-v2, gpt2, roberta-base, t5-small, xlm-roberta-base, TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat-v1.0, codegen-350M-mono and phi-2. Each model got 12 to 14 texts with accents, extra spaces and line breaks, CJK characters, emoji, code and special tokens. I also checked a pair of texts for BERT, and truncation. Every check passed. Apart from the BERT cases of #7724 and #7725, which #7820 has since fixed on main, the only differences from Hugging Face are the ones the guide describes.
- I also pasted each example into a new .NET 10 console app (13 apps), with Microsoft.ML.Tokenizers 3.0.0 from `dotnet add package` and the model files from Hugging Face. This included the GPT-2, Phi-2 and RoBERTa variants that the text describes. The apps build without warnings, every ID in the guide's comments matches, and 64 of the 67 outputs are the same as in `transformers` 5.24.0. The other 3 are the BERT line-break case of #7724, which #7820 has since fixed on main. The Python sample prints the IDs in its comment.

## Not in this PR

- Guidance on running Hugging Face models with ONNX, TorchSharp or System.Numerics.Tensors, which #7384 also asks for. That's why this PR says "Contributes to" rather than "Fixes".
- A factory that finds and loads the right tokenizer from a model's files. That's #7735.

Issues.Title: Make BertTokenizer strip accents in globalization-invariant mode
Issues.Body:
Fixes #7728

`BertOptions.RemoveNonSpacingMarks` strips accents with `string.Normalize(NormalizationForm.FormD)`. In globalization-invariant mode `string.Normalize` returns its input unchanged, so the accents stay and, with uncased vocabularies, words like "café" become `[UNK]`. Invariant mode is common: the Native AOT templates and the default Alpine and chiseled container images turn it on.

## Changes

- When `string.Normalize` doesn't work, `BertNormalizer` removes the accents using a table instead. For each character whose canonical decomposition contains non-spacing marks, the table holds the character without them (é → e). Nothing changes when ICU or NLS is available.
- There's no public API to detect invariant mode yet (dotnet/runtime#81429), so it checks whether `Normalize` decomposes "é".
- The table (991 characters, about 8 KB) is generated from the Unicode Character Database 18.0.0 by a small tool in `tools-local/GenerateNonSpacingMarkTable`. As with the Unicode tables in dotnet/runtime, the tool isn't part of the build, and its Readme explains how to update the table.
- I added the Unicode license to THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.TXT, since the table comes from Unicode data.

Accent stripping shouldn't depend on the environment, and in Hugging Face it doesn't: its Python BERT tokenizer uses Python's built-in `unicodedata`, and its Rust tokenizers use the `unicode-normalization` crate. Both carry their own Unicode data, so the same text gives the same tokens on every machine.

I didn't go with the issue's other option, throwing from `BertTokenizer.Create` in invariant mode. It would break apps that work today because their text has no accents, and it still wouldn't give the right tokens.

## Tests

Two new tests run `BertTokenizer` in a separate process with invariant mode on (RemoteExecutor). One repeats the accent cases of `TestWithAccentMarks` and checks that characters without marks, like ß and Ø, are kept; the other checks that every character whose decomposition contains non-spacing marks gives the same result as with ICU. Both fail without the fix. They only run on .NET, as .NET Framework has no invariant mode.

## Not in this PR

The tokenizer.json `StripAccents` and `NFC`/`NFD`/`NFKC`/`NFKD` normalizer steps have the same problem in invariant mode. They're left for a separate change.

Characters that Unicode normalization changes without removing any marks, like CJK compatibility ideographs (U+F900 → U+8C48) or the Kelvin sign (U+212A → K), still aren't normalized in invariant mode, with or without `RemoveNonSpacingMarks`. That was already the case, and the table only covers characters with marks.

<details>
<summary>Checking the table with Python</summary>

This prints the table's mapping using Python's own Unicode data. Python 3.11 has Unicode 14, so its output doesn't include the table's 3 newer characters (U+105C9, U+105E4 and U+11385).

```python
import unicodedata as ud

for cp in range(0x110000):
    c = chr(cp)
    if ud.category(c) in ('Mn', 'Cs'):
        continue
    d = ud.normalize('NFD', c)
    if any(ud.category(x) == 'Mn' for x in d):
        r = ud.normalize('NFC', ''.join(x for x in d if ud.category(x) != 'Mn'))
        if r != c:
            print(f'U+{cp:04X} -> {" ".join(f"U+{ord(x):04X}" for x in r)}')
```

</details>

Issues.Title: [Draft] Breaking changes in ML.NET 7.0: Linux x64 OpenMP library name and glibc compatibility
Issues.Body:
> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Draft — subject to change.** This notice describes planned changes and has not been approved by the ML.NET maintainers. Details, versions and guidance may change before release. Feedback is welcome.

# Breaking changes: Linux native dependencies in ML.NET 7.0

The next major version of ML.NET (assumed to be **7.0.0**) changes how its Linux native libraries are built. This has two customer-visible effects:

1. **x64 OpenMP library name:** On Linux x64, Symbolic SGD now loads `libomp.so.5` instead of `libomp.so`, the same name arm and arm64 already use.
2. **glibc compatibility:** All Linux native assets now target the same glibc distro eras as the .NET 10 build. Some arm and arm64 assets now require newer distros.

There are no managed API changes. The packages' target frameworks don't change.

## Background

ML.NET's Linux native assets were built two different ways:

| RID | Previous build | New build |
|---|---|---|
| linux-x64 | Native build in a CentOS Stream 8 container (end of life, image no longer maintained) | Cross-build against an Ubuntu 18.04 sysroot |
| linux-arm64 | Cross-build against an Ubuntu 16.04 sysroot (.NET 8 era) | Cross-build against an Ubuntu 18.04 sysroot |
| linux-arm | Cross-build against an Ubuntu 16.04 sysroot (.NET 8 era) | Cross-build against an Ubuntu 22.04 sysroot |

The new builds use the Azure Linux 4 .NET 11 cross-build images, which dotnet/runtime also uses. The build host is a current, maintained OS; the target sysroot determines which distros the binaries run on. For background, see dotnet/runtime#83428 and dotnet/runtime#109939, and the [Linux build methodology](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/docs/project/linux-build-methodology.md). Tracking issue: #7925.

## Change 1: x64 OpenMP library name (`libomp.so` → `libomp.so.5`)

### Previous behavior

On Linux x64, `libSymSgdNative.so` (`Microsoft.ML.Mkl.Components`) depended on `libomp.so`, the unversioned name used by RHEL-family distros. On arm and arm64 it already depended on `libomp.so.5`.

### New behavior

On every Linux architecture, `libSymSgdNative.so` depends on `libomp.so.5`. Both names refer to the same LLVM OpenMP runtime; only the file name the loader looks for has changed.

This doesn't change the existing x64 Intel MKL dependency: `libMklImports.so` still requires `libiomp5.so`.

### Who is affected

Linux x64 apps that use Symbolic SGD on a system that provides `libomp.so` but not `libomp.so.5`, including Azure Linux, Fedora and RHEL-compatible distros. On those systems the load fails with an error like this:

```text
libomp.so.5: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
```

Debian and Ubuntu install `libomp.so.5` on the default library path with the `libomp5` package. The released x64 binary needed `libomp.so`, which those distros put only under an LLVM-specific directory, not the default library path, so this change makes the x64 asset easier to use there.

### How to update your environment

**Debian and Ubuntu**

```bash
sudo apt-get install -y libomp5      # provides libomp.so.5
sudo apt-get install -y libomp-dev   # x64 Intel MKL components: provides libiomp5.so
```

Verified on Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12.

**Azure Linux, Fedora, RHEL, AlmaLinux and other RHEL-compatible distros**

These distros ship the LLVM OpenMP runtime as `/usr/lib64/libomp.so` only; `libomp-devel` doesn't add `libomp.so.5`. Install `libomp`, then create the expected names, either next to your app or system-wide.

App-local (no system changes; good for containers and app deployments):

```bash
sudo dnf install -y libomp        # tdnf on Azure Linux
ln -s /usr/lib64/libomp.so <app-dir>/libomp.so.5
ln -s /usr/lib64/libomp.so <app-dir>/libiomp5.so   # x64 Intel MKL components only
```

System-wide:

```bash
sudo dnf install -y libomp        # tdnf on Azure Linux
sudo ln -s libomp.so /usr/lib64/libomp.so.5
sudo ln -s libomp.so /usr/lib64/libiomp5.so          # x64 Intel MKL components only
sudo ldconfig
```

For example, a Dockerfile for an app image:

```dockerfile
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/runtime:10.0-azurelinux4.0
RUN tdnf install -y libomp && tdnf clean all \
    && ln -s libomp.so /usr/lib64/libomp.so.5 \
    && ln -s libomp.so /usr/lib64/libiomp5.so
```

Azure Linux 3 doesn't provide an LLVM OpenMP (`libomp`) package, so Symbolic SGD needs another OpenMP source there (or use Azure Linux 4). This applies to 6.0.0 as well.

This guidance was validated with a Symbolic SGD train-and-evaluate smoke test (self-contained .NET 10 app) on Azure Linux 4, Fedora 43, and AlmaLinux 9 and 10, on x64 and arm64, using both app-local and system-wide links: https://github.com/richlander/machinelearning/actions/runs/45556406022

Note that released 6.0.0 Symbolic SGD also fails on these distros with only `libomp` installed: arm64 can't find `libomp.so.5`, and x64 can't find MKL's `libiomp5.so`. The same links fix both versions.

The same guidance is being added to [platform-limitations.md](https://github.com/dotnet/machinelearning/blob/main/docs/project-docs/platform-limitations.md) in #7946.

## Change 2: glibc compatibility

### Key point: distro era, not .NET version

ML.NET packages still target the same frameworks. **Which .NET versions can use ML.NET is unchanged.** If your app can reference ML.NET 6.0 today, it can reference ML.NET 7.0.

What changes is the oldest Linux distro on which the **native** assets load. That's determined by the glibc version in the cross-build sysroot. It's independent of which .NET runtime the app uses.

- ML.NET 6.0 built arm and arm64 against a .NET 8-era sysroot (Ubuntu 16.04).
- ML.NET 7.0 builds against the .NET 10-era sysroots: Ubuntu 18.04 for x64 and arm64, and Ubuntu 22.04 for arm (the [arm32 Y2038 baseline](https://github.com/dotnet/core/discussions/9285)).

For example, a .NET 8 app using ML.NET 7.0 on Ubuntu 16.04 arm64 still runs .NET, but ML.NET's native assets fail to load because the distro's glibc is too old. The same app on Ubuntu 18.04 or later works. The minimums are the same as .NET 10's, so any distro that .NET 10 supports can run these assets.

### New minimums

| RID | Minimum compatible distro era | glibc |
|---|---|---|
| linux-x64 | Ubuntu 18.04 | 2.27 (unchanged in practice) |
| linux-arm64 | Ubuntu 18.04 | 2.27 (was 2.17) |
| linux-arm | Ubuntu 22.04 | 2.35 (was 2.4) |

Compatible glibc distros include (at the version shown or later): Ubuntu 18.04 (arm: 22.04), Debian 11 (arm: 12), RHEL / AlmaLinux 8, CentOS Stream 9, Amazon Linux 2023, Fedora 38, and Azure Linux 3. See dotnet/runtime#109939 for more distro glibc versions.

Measured changes in the candidate native assets, compared with the released 6.0.0 packages:

| Asset | 6.0.0 → 7.0 candidate |
|---|---|
| x64 SymSGD | `GLIBC_2.27` unchanged (and `libomp.so` → `libomp.so.5`, see change 1) |
| arm64 SymSGD and MatrixFactorization | `GLIBC_2.17` → `GLIBC_2.27` |
| arm64 Lda and MatrixFactorization | `GLIBCXX_3.4.21` → `GLIBCXX_3.4.22` |
| arm SymSGD | `GLIBC_2.4` → `GLIBC_2.27`; `GLIBCXX_3.4.21` → `GLIBCXX_3.4.29` |
| arm Lda and MatrixFactorization | `GLIBC_2.4` → `GLIBC_2.32`; `GLIBCXX_3.4.21` → `GLIBCXX_3.4.30` |

ELF comparison of the native and MKL libraries against the released packages: https://github.com/richlander/machinelearning/actions/runs/45548312386

### Who is affected

- Apps on **arm64** distros with glibc older than 2.27 (for example, Ubuntu 16.04).
- Apps on **arm32** distros older than the Ubuntu 22.04 era, such as Debian 10/11, Ubuntu 20.04, and Raspberry Pi OS based on Debian 11. .NET 9 and later already require this baseline on arm32.

### Recommended action

Run on a distro at or above the minimums above. If you can't upgrade the OS, stay on ML.NET 6.x.

To check a system's glibc version:

```bash
ldd --version
```

## Affected packages

Packages with Linux native assets (checked against the latest released versions):

| Package | Linux native asset | Change 1 (OpenMP) | Change 2 (glibc) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Microsoft.ML` 6.0.0 | `libLdaNative.so` | No | Yes (arm, arm64) |
| `Microsoft.ML.Mkl.Components` 6.0.0 | `libSymSgdNative.so` | Yes (x64) | Yes (arm, arm64) |
| `Microsoft.ML.Recommender` 0.24.0 | `libMatrixFactorizationNative.so` | No | Yes (arm, arm64) |

`Microsoft.ML.Recommender` is versioned separately (0.x), so its next version would be the equivalent major update for that package.

## Status

- [x] PR/CI cross-builds moved to Azure Linux 4 (#7926)
- [ ] Official builds moved to Azure Linux 4 (#7946)
- [ ] Release-build tests on Ubuntu/Debian with the candidate assets
- [ ] Maintainer approval of this notice

Issues.Title: Progress subchannel constructor receives the ID and nesting level in reverse order
Issues.Body:
On current main `a3d5f26654803cdd3851a5cacda97e483d890373`, `ProgressChannel.StartProgressChannel(int level)` calls `new SubChannel(this, level, newId)`, while the constructor takes `(root, id, level)`.

Creating a second root child therefore reuses ID 1 and fails the duplicate-channel assertion in Debug.
The unique channel ID is also used as its nesting level, although progress entries are ordered by nesting level.

I would like to correct the argument order and add a regression covering sibling channels, a nested child, progress aggregation and independent disposal.
The regression fails at the duplicate-channel assertion before the fix and passes on .NET 10 and .NET 11 afterward.

The root build is blocked on this Linux host by missing Clang/native libraries.
The focused managed regression was built and executed using an external target that skips native-library copies and enables the test framework's existing `SKIP_MKL` initialization switch; neither setting is part of the proposed repository change.

Issues.Title: Preserve progress subchannel identity and nesting level
Issues.Body:
Fixes #7941.

Creating multiple progress channels at the same depth currently reuses the depth as their dictionary ID and stores the unique ID as the nesting level.
Pass `(root, newId, level)` to `SubChannel` so sibling channels remain independent and progress is ordered by actual nesting depth.

The regression covers sibling and nested channels, aggregated metric values, and disposal without removing another channel's progress.
It fails at the duplicate-ID assertion before the fix and passes on both net10.0 and net11.0 afterward.

The root build could not complete because this Linux host lacks Clang/native libraries.
Focused managed tests were built with an external target that skips native copies and enables the test framework's existing `SKIP_MKL` switch; the override is outside the repository and is not included in this PR.

Issues.Title: Use UTF-8 for DataFrame CSV output
Issues.Body:

Issues.Title: ExceptParamValue swaps the exception parameter name and message
Issues.Body:
The two non-formatting `Contracts.ExceptParamValue<T>` overloads pass `(msg, value, paramName)` to `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`, whose constructor expects `(paramName, actualValue, message)`.

For example, `Contracts.ExceptParamValue(-7, "count", "Count must be positive.")` sets `ParamName` to `"Count must be positive."` and uses `"count"` as the message.
The overload with an `IExceptionContext` has the same behavior.
Both formatting overloads already use the correct order.

Confirmed on main at a3d5f26654803cdd3851a5cacda97e483d890373.
A two-case regression fails on the original code and passes with the arguments corrected.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "ExceptParamValue swaps the exception parameter name and message" (#7943)

Issues.Title: Fix exception parameter names and messages
Issues.Body:
Fixes #7943.

Pass `(paramName, value, msg)` when constructing exceptions in both non-formatting `ExceptParamValue` overloads.
Previously, the error message became `ParamName` and the parameter name became the message.
The regression checks the name, value, and message with and without an exception context; all three `TestContracts` cases pass on net10.0 and net11.0.

The host lacks Clang/native libraries, so the root build could not complete.
These managed tests use an external native-copy override and the test framework's existing `SKIP_MKL` switch; neither changes the submitted code.

Issues.Title: Move official Linux builds to Azure Linux 4
Issues.Body:
## Summary

- Move the official Linux x64, arm and arm64 native-package builds to the same Azure Linux 4 .NET 11 cross images, sysroots and linker as PR CI.
- Preserve the existing build-agent pool, package-asset steps and signing pipeline.
- Document how Azure Linux, Fedora and RHEL-family consumers provide the OpenMP runtime names ML.NET loads.

Part of #7925. There are no managed public API changes.

## Why: one targeting model across architectures

Today the official x64 build runs natively on CentOS Stream 8, while arm and arm64 cross-build against Ubuntu sysroots. Shipped assets therefore differ by architecture: x64 SymSGD loads `libomp.so`, arm/arm64 SymSGD load `libomp.so.5`. After this change, all architectures build against the .NET sysroots (Ubuntu 18.04 for x64/arm64, Ubuntu 22.04 for arm), so the native floors and the consumer guidance are the same everywhere.

## Dependency and review

Depends on #7926. Because both branches are in a fork, this PR targets `main` and initially includes the #7926 commits. Merge #7926 first, then update this branch from `main` so its diff shows only the official-build changes.

## Compatibility

**glibc/libstdc++ floors** now match the .NET 10–12 support baseline ([supported-os](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/main/release-notes/10.0/supported-os.md)): glibc 2.27 for x64/arm64, glibc 2.35 (Ubuntu 22.04, Y2038) for arm. No candidate asset exceeds those floors.

| Asset | Released → candidate |
|---|---|
| x64 SymSGD | `libomp.so` → `libomp.so.5` (now matches arm/arm64); `GLIBC_2.27` unchanged |
| arm64 SymSGD and MatrixFactorization | `GLIBC_2.17` → `GLIBC_2.27` |
| arm64 Lda and MatrixFactorization | `GLIBCXX_3.4.21` → `GLIBCXX_3.4.22` |
| arm SymSGD | `GLIBC_2.4` → `GLIBC_2.27`; `GLIBCXX_3.4.21` → `GLIBCXX_3.4.29` |
| arm Lda and MatrixFactorization | `GLIBC_2.4` → `GLIBC_2.32`; `GLIBCXX_3.4.21` → `GLIBCXX_3.4.30` |

**OpenMP on RHEL-family distros.** Azure Linux, Fedora and RHEL-compatible distros ship LLVM OpenMP as `libomp.so` only. Released 6.0.0 SymSGD already fails there out of the box (arm64: missing `libomp.so.5`; x64: MKL's missing `libiomp5.so`). This PR documents a guidance fix in `docs/project-docs/platform-limitations.md`: install `libomp` and link `libomp.so.5` (and `libiomp5.so` on x64) to it, app-local or system-wide.

SymSGD smoke test (train + evaluate, self-contained .NET 10 app): https://github.com/richlander/machinelearning/actions/runs/45556406022

| | Azure Linux 4 | Fedora 43 | AlmaLinux 9 | AlmaLinux 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| x64 released / candidate, `libomp` only | fail / fail | fail / fail | fail / fail | fail / fail |
| x64 candidate, app-local links | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| x64 candidate, system links | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| arm64 released / candidate, `libomp` only | fail / fail | fail / fail | fail / fail | fail / fail |
| arm64 candidate, app-local links | pass | pass | pass | pass |
| arm64 candidate, system links | pass | pass | pass | pass |

`libomp-devel` does not provide `libomp.so.5`, so installing it is not sufficient.

## Validation

- [x] Pipeline images, sysroots and linker flags match PR CI for all three official jobs.
- [x] Release native-package builds for x64, arm and arm64: https://github.com/richlander/machinelearning/actions/runs/45547780465
- [x] Direct ELF comparison of 14 native/MKL libraries against released packages: https://github.com/richlander/machinelearning/actions/runs/45548312386
- [x] SymSGD functional smoke test with the documented guidance on Azure Linux 4, Fedora 43, AlmaLinux 9/10 (x64, arm64): https://github.com/richlander/machinelearning/actions/runs/45556406022
- [ ] Run relevant tests on Ubuntu/Debian with the candidate assets.
- [ ] Validate the signed official pipeline before merging.
